Ice Age History for Sleep 🌙 How Did Ancient Humans Sleep?

About 1 hour 58 min · Released Mon 26 Oct 2026 · Updated 9 Nov 2026 · narrated slowly for sleep

Watch on YouTube Listen on YouTube Music

How did ancient humans sleep? A bedtime story for grown-ups in calming history narration: relaxing bedtime history from one long Ice Age night.

Nobody wrote anything down in the Ice Age, so this episode tries to show where the evidence stops. The grass beds of Border Cave and Sibudu, the mammoth-bone houses and the sleep studies of the Hadza, San and Tsimane are real; the family, their dog and their stories are imagined. Where researchers disagree, as on early cooking or Roger Ekirch's "first sleep", the narration says so.

What about Supper by the Hearth?

It's time to eat. The mother hands the baby to the grandmother for a moment, and kneels by the hearth. Near the edge of the fire, where the stones are hot but the flames don't reach, she's set several flat stones to warm, and now she lays thin strips of meat across them. The meat sizzles at once, with a soft, spitting hiss, and a smell rises up that fills the whole house. It's rich and smoky and good, and the children, who have been lying on the furs looking sleepy, sit up straight.

What about Needles and Furs?

The evening meal is over now, and the house has grown quieter. The children are full and warm, and the little girl has climbed into her mother's lap and is half asleep already, one hand curled around a fold of her mother's coat. The grandmother has taken up some work. She's sewing. Watch her hands, because what she's doing is one of the great inventions of the human past, and without it, no one could have slept through a night like this one.

What about Nests in the Trees?

While the house settles into sleep, let's drift a long way back again, further than the grass beds of Border Cave, further than the first fires. Let's ask where human sleep began. To do that, we have to go to the forests of Africa, and look up into the trees. It's evening in a forest, somewhere in the centre of the continent, and the light is green and gold, filtering down through layer after layer of leaves. High in the branches of a tall tree, perhaps fifty or sixty feet above the ground, a chimpanzee is making her bed.

What about Sleeping Close?

Let's look around the house now, in the low red light, and see how everyone is sleeping. They're sleeping close. The house is small, and there are eight people in it, and they lie near enough to each other that, if any one of them stretched out an arm, they'd touch someone else. The mother lies with the baby tucked against her chest, and the little girl curled at her back. The father lies with the boy beside him. The young man lies near the door, between the sleepers and the cold.

What about the Watcher by the Fire?

Not everyone in the camp is asleep. In the house next to ours, an older man is sitting up by his fire. He's wrapped in a heavy robe, with his knees drawn up and his arms around them, and he's looking into the embers, wide awake. He isn't anxious, and he isn't on guard, exactly. He just isn't sleepy. He went to sleep early in the evening, before the stories were finished, and now, in the middle of the night, he's woken, as he often does, and he's sitting by the fire for a while, keeping it alive, listening to the night.

What the Sleepers Taught Us?

The older man stands in the doorway, and the cold air flows in past him, and he looks out at the night. Let's leave him there for a little while, looking at the stars, and think about another study of sleep, a larger one, because it tells us something lovely about the shape of a human night. In 2015, a team of researchers led by Gandhi Yetish and Jerome Siegel, at the University of California, Los Angeles, published the results of a careful study.

What about First Sleep and Second Sleep?

There's a question that many people ask when they wonder how our ancestors slept, and it's worth taking slowly. Did people once sleep in two parts? The idea comes from the work of a historian named Roger Ekirch. In the 1990s and early two thousands, Ekirch was studying how people in Europe lived at night, in the centuries before electric light. He read hundreds and hundreds of old documents, diaries, letters, court records, medical books, prayer books and poems, many of them from the 1500s to the 1800s.

0:00:00Intro · 621 words

A small fire glows inside a round house built of bones. Outside, the wind moves across a wide, frozen plain, and the stars are so many and so bright that the sky looks dusted with frost. A mother pulls a fur up over a sleeping child. Someone leans forward and lays one more stick on the embers, and the light rises, warm and gold, across the curved walls. It's about eighteen thousand years ago, as the coldest part of the last Ice Age is just beginning to ease, and the long night is just beginning.

Intro

Hello, and welcome to Dreaming Ages History. Tonight we go further back than we've ever gone before. We're going to spend one whole night with some of the very first people who slept as we sleep, from the last light of a winter evening to the first grey light of morning, somewhere on the great cold plains of the last Ice Age.

Tonight's question is a simple one, and a very old one. How did ancient humans sleep? Where did they lay their heads, what kept them warm, and who kept watch while the others dreamed? Did they sleep in one long stretch, as many of us try to, or in two parts, with a quiet time of waking in between? And how far back does the story of human sleep really go?

We should say clearly what's real and what's imagined. The little family we'll spend the night with is invented. We don't know their names, their language, or the words of their stories, and we never will. But the world around them is built from things that archaeologists have found and studied with great care. We have the houses they built from the bones of mammoths, the hearths where their fires burned, the needles they used to sew their clothes, the lamps they carved from stone, and the beds of grass and leaves that people laid down in caves many thousands of years earlier still. We also have the patient work of scientists who have studied how people sleep today in a few places without electric light. Where the evidence is strong, we'll say so. Where it's uncertain, or where scholars disagree, we'll say that too. And where we're simply picturing a scene, we'll tell you.

Our night takes place on what scientists call the mammoth steppe, a vast cold grassland that once stretched across much of Europe and Asia. Our family lives near a river, in a land that today lies in eastern Europe. It's late in the year. The ground is hard with frost, the grass is pale and dry, and herds of mammoth, reindeer, horse and bison have moved across the plain all summer and autumn.

As we go, keep one thing in mind: the hearth. All through the night, someone will feed the fire, a stick at a time, and the fire will breathe, and glow, and sink, and rise again. For hundreds of thousands of years, before there were clocks or bells or calendars, the fire was the heart of every human night. Tonight we'll keep coming back to it, the way a sleeper wakes for a moment in the dark, sees the soft red glow of the embers, and drifts off again.

Now settle in, let your shoulders drop, and let your breathing slow. Let the room grow quiet around you. Imagine the weight of a thick, soft fur across your legs, and the gentle warmth of a fire close by. There's no danger tonight, and no hurry, only a soft voice, a sleeping camp, and the long, slow turning of the stars.

Our night begins out on the open steppe, just as the sun is going down.

0:00:56Dusk on the Mammoth Steppe · 1,150 words

The sun is low now, and very red, resting just above the flat edge of the world. There are no hills to hide it and no trees to break the light. The whole plain stretches away from you in every direction, pale gold and grey, and the low sun lays a long, rosy shine across it, so that every tuft of frozen grass casts a little blue shadow behind it.

You're standing on a gentle rise above a river. The river is wide and slow, and at its edges it has already begun to freeze. A thin skin of ice reaches out from the banks, white and glassy, and in the middle the dark water still moves, quietly, carrying a few small floating plates of ice downstream. Along the bank there are a few low, bare willow bushes and a scattering of birch, their thin branches bending in the wind. Apart from these, there are hardly any trees at all.

The air is cold, colder than almost any evening you've known. When you breathe in, it touches the back of your throat, clean and sharp, and when you breathe out, your breath hangs in front of you in a small white cloud and slowly fades. The wind isn't strong tonight. It comes steadily from the north, across hundreds of miles of open grass, and it smells of nothing at all except cold, and a faint sweetness of dry grass, and, very far away, a trace of smoke.

This is the mammoth steppe. Eighteen thousand years ago, the world was in the closing part of the last great Ice Age. Huge sheets of ice still lay over much of northern Europe and North America, more than a mile thick in places, though they had begun, very slowly, to melt. So much water was locked up in that ice that the seas were lower than they are today, and coastlines were further out. South of the ice, across a great belt of land from the Atlantic to Siberia and on into Alaska, there spread a cold, dry grassland. It was too dry for thick forest, and too cold for many of the plants we know. But it was rich in grasses, sedges and low herbs, and it fed enormous herds of grazing animals.

Out across the plain, a long way off, you can see some of them now. A line of dark shapes moves slowly along the far side of the river, heads low, grazing as they go. They're horses, small and stocky, with thick winter coats and short, upright manes. Further still, almost at the edge of sight, there's a group of much larger shapes, rounded and shaggy, moving even more slowly. Woolly mammoths. They're not as tall as you might imagine, perhaps about as tall as a modern African elephant, or a little less, but they're wrapped in long, dark, coarse hair, and their great curved tusks catch the red light of the sun. They're walking away from you, unhurried, the way they've walked across this land for many thousands of years.

Closer in, the frozen ground is marked with the trails of other animals. There are the neat, split prints of reindeer, and the round pads of an arctic fox, and the long, scratching lines where a hare has run. Somewhere in the grass, a small bird calls once and is silent.

Now turn around, and look down the other side of the rise. There, near the river, but up on a dry terrace where the spring floods won't reach, is the camp.

At first, it hardly looks like a camp at all. You see four or five low, round mounds, a little like small hills, each one rising out of the ground to about the height of a person, perhaps a little more. They're dark, and their sides are rough and lumpy, and here and there something pale shows through, curved and smooth, like the edge of a great shell. From the top of one of the mounds, a thin thread of grey smoke rises straight up for a moment, then bends in the wind and drifts away south.

Around the mounds, there are signs of the day's work. A few skins are stretched on frames of wood and bone to dry. A heap of firewood, mostly thin sticks of willow and birch, and some heavy pale pieces of bone, sits by one doorway. There are pits dug into the frozen ground, and some are covered with skins and weighted with stones. That's where food is kept. In this cold, the ground itself is a store, and meat buried there in autumn will stay frozen until spring.

A few people are still outside. They're bundled in clothes of fur and hide, sewn close to the body, with hoods drawn up. It's hard to tell much about them from here. One is carrying an armful of sticks toward a doorway. Another is crouched by a drying frame, rolling up a stiff hide. A child, very small and round in a fur suit, runs a few steps after a dog, and is called back by a voice you can't understand, and turns, and goes.

That dog, by the way, is something we have to be careful about. People and wolves had certainly begun to come together by around this time, and some of the oldest bones that scientists think belonged to early dogs are found at camps like this one, on the plains of eastern and central Europe. But exactly when and where wolves first became dogs is still argued about, and the earliest examples are disputed. So let's say this softly. In our camp tonight, there's a dog, or something close to one, and it's a quiet, watchful animal that sleeps near the fire. We're picturing that, but it's a reasonable picture.

The sun touches the edge of the plain now. For a moment, it seems to rest there, flattened and glowing, and the whole sky above it turns pink and gold and then pale green. Then it begins to sink. The light draws back across the grass, and the long blue shadows join together and become one great shadow, and the cold deepens all at once, as if someone had opened a door.

The people outside finish their work. The one with the hide carries it in. The one with the sticks bends low and pushes through the doorway of the nearest mound, and the hide that covers the doorway falls closed behind them. For a second, as it opens and shuts, you see a glimpse of orange light inside, and then it's gone.

Above you, the first star appears. Then another. Then, quite suddenly, there are dozens of them, and the sky, which was green a moment ago, is a deep, clear blue, and darkening fast.

The night has begun. Let's go inside, out of the wind.

0:10:31The House of Bones · 1,270 words

You bend down low, almost to your knees, and push aside the heavy hide that hangs over the doorway. It's stiff with cold on the outside and soft on the inside, and it smells of smoke and animal. Beyond it there's a short passage, dug a little way down into the ground, so that you step down as you go in. Then a second hide, and you push through that too, and you're inside.

The first thing you notice is the warmth. It isn't the warmth of a modern room. It's closer and more alive than that, a warmth that comes in waves from the fire in the middle of the floor and from the bodies of the people around it. After the bitter cold outside, it wraps around your face and hands like a blanket, and your skin begins to tingle.

The second thing you notice is the smell. Wood smoke, and burning fat, and the deep, earthy smell of furs and hides, and of people who have worked hard all day. Underneath it all, there's something sweeter and drier, the smell of grass and herbs.

Then your eyes begin to adjust to the light, and you look up, and around, and you see the walls.

They're made of bones. Huge bones. Mammoth bones, stacked and fitted together with great care. Around the base of the wall, set into the ground, there's a ring of great mammoth skulls, heavy and rounded, each one as big as a large boulder. On top of them, and between them, there are long leg bones, standing upright or laid crossways, and jaw bones, dozens of them, stacked one into another so that they make a kind of rippled pattern, like rows of waves. Higher up, there are shoulder blades and pelvis bones, broad and flat. And over the doorway, curving across it in a great pale arch, there are two long tusks, set so that their tips meet.

The bones aren't bare. Between them and over them, the walls are covered with something dark, and in places you can see that it's hide, layers of animal skin, laid over the bone frame and held down. Earth and turf may have been packed against the outside too, to keep out the wind. We don't know exactly how each house was covered, but something like this would have been needed to make it warm. The bones are the frame, the strong skeleton of the house, and the hides are its skin.

Houses like this one are real. Archaeologists have found the remains of them at a number of sites across the plains of what are now Ukraine, Russia, Belarus and Poland. One of the best known is at a place called Mezhyrich, near where two rivers meet, south of Kyiv. There, in the 1960s, a farmer digging a cellar struck a mammoth jaw bone, and the excavations that followed uncovered the remains of several round houses built of mammoth bones. For a long time the Mezhyrich houses were thought to be about fifteen thousand years old, but a new study in 2025, using fresh radiocarbon dates, placed one of them at around eighteen thousand years ago, and that's the time we've chosen for our imagined camp tonight. Altogether, the site held the bones of something like a hundred and fifty mammoths. Some other bone houses and rings on these plains are older still. A great ring of mammoth bones at a place called Kostenki, near the river Don in Russia, has been dated to around twenty five thousand years ago, in the coldest part of the Ice Age, though it may have been used for storage or gatherings rather than as a home.

Did these people hunt all those mammoths? Probably not all of them. Many of the bones may have been collected from animals that died naturally, gathered from riverbanks and old kill sites, perhaps over many years. Bone was precious here. On a plain with so few trees, a mammoth's skeleton was timber, and fuel, and tools, all at once. We'll come back to that when we talk about the fire.

The house is round, and not very large. If you stretched out your arms and walked from one side to the other, you might take six or seven steps. The floor is dug a little way into the ground, which helps to keep the warmth in, and the ground beneath you is packed hard and smooth from use. It's covered here and there with skins and mats of woven grass, and in some places with a soft, springy layer of something dry and fragrant.

In the middle of the floor is the hearth.

It's a shallow pit, lined with stones, and in it a small fire is burning, low and bright. It's not a roaring fire. It's a careful, sensible fire, just big enough to light the house and warm the air, with a few sticks of willow crackling quietly and a large, pale piece of bone glowing red underneath them. Above it, in the roof, there's a small opening, and the smoke rises up toward it, slowly, in a soft grey column, and goes out into the night. Not all of it, though. Some of the smoke stays, and hangs in the curve of the roof, and gives the whole house a faint blue haze, so that the light from the fire seems to glow inside the air itself.

Around the fire, there are the people.

There are perhaps seven or eight of them in this house tonight. That's our family, and we'll get to know them a little. There's a grandmother, small and wrinkled, sitting very close to the fire with a fur around her shoulders. There's a man and a woman of middle age, and a younger woman with a baby, and two children, a boy of about eight and a girl of about five, and a young man, perhaps sixteen or seventeen, who has just come in with the firewood. We'll call them by what they are, the grandmother, the mother, the father, and so on, because we don't know their names. Other families live in the other houses close by, and between them, the whole camp is perhaps thirty or forty people.

They're people just like us. That's important to say. These are fully modern humans, the same species as you and me, with the same kinds of minds and the same kinds of feelings. If you could bring that baby forward through eighteen thousand years and raise her in a city today, she would grow up speaking a modern language, going to school, and laughing at the same kinds of jokes as everyone else. These people aren't simpler than us. They simply know different things. They know how to read the tracks of a hundred animals, how to find their way across a plain with no roads, how to make a needle, how to sew a coat that will keep you alive at forty degrees below zero, and how to keep a fire burning through the longest night of the year.

The young man sets down his armful of sticks by the wall, near the door, and crouches beside the fire to warm his hands. He holds them out flat, palms toward the flames, and you can see the red light glowing through the edges of his fingers. The grandmother says something to him, softly, and he smiles, and nods, and reaches for a stick, and lays it on the fire.

The flames rise a little, and the shadows of the bones move on the walls.

0:19:05Gathering the Fire · 1,119 words

Let's sit down by the fire for a while, close enough to feel it on your face, and watch it burn.

It's a simple thing, a small fire in a pit of stones. But it may be the most important thing in the whole story of human sleep. Without it, these people couldn't live here at all. With it, they can live almost anywhere.

Look at what's burning. There are sticks of willow and birch, gathered from along the river. They burn quickly, with a bright, clear flame, and they crackle and spit a little as the sap boils inside them. But wood is scarce on the steppe, and these sticks won't last long. So underneath them, in the heart of the fire, there's bone. Large pieces of mammoth bone, and the bones of horse and reindeer, broken open and laid in the embers.

Burning bone is something you might never have seen. Fresh bone is full of fat, especially the inner, spongy part, and that fat burns, slowly and steadily, with a low, yellow flame. Once a bone fire gets going, it can give heat for a long time, and the bones glow red and then white as they burn. Archaeologists find huge amounts of burned bone in the hearths of Ice Age camps on these plains, and they think that in places where wood was very scarce, bone was one of the main fuels. It doesn't smell of wood smoke, exactly. It smells of something richer and heavier, a little like a roast that's been left too long. But the people here are used to it. To them, it's simply the smell of home.

Now let's go much further back. Let's ask where this fire came from.

No one knows exactly when people first began to use fire. It's one of the great questions of the deep past, and the answer keeps moving as new evidence is found. But here's what we can say.

Our story begins in Africa, a very long time ago. More than two million years ago, there were early members of the human family walking on two legs across the grasslands and woodlands of Africa. They made simple stone tools, and they ate meat as well as plants. Fire was all around them, in a way. Lightning would strike the dry grass in the hot season, and wildfires would sweep across the land. After a fire, there would be cooked animals and roasted seeds and roots left behind on the blackened ground, and perhaps those early people learned to look for them.

At some point, they began to do more than that. They began to carry fire, and to keep it. In a cave called Wonderwerk, in South Africa, scientists have found tiny pieces of burned bone and ash from plants, deep inside the cave, in layers that are thought to be about a million years old. Because they're so far inside, it's very unlikely that a wildfire blew them in. Many scientists think this is some of the earliest good evidence that human ancestors were using fire in a controlled way. There are other claims that are older still, from sites in East Africa, but those are harder to prove, because it's difficult to tell a campfire from a natural burn after so long. So let's say this. By around a million years ago, and perhaps earlier, some of our ancestors were living with fire.

Later, the evidence becomes stronger. At a site in Israel, by the shore of an ancient lake, there are layers dated to about seven hundred and eighty thousand years ago with clusters of burned flint and burned seeds and wood, in patterns that suggest hearths. By around four hundred thousand years ago, fire seems to have become a regular part of life in many places, and by the time our own species appears, it seems to be widespread.

So what did fire do for sleep?

First, of course, it gave warmth. A fire let people sleep in places and in seasons that would otherwise have been far too cold. It's not too much to say that fire, together with clothing, is what let humans walk out of the warm places of Africa and live on the cold plains of Europe and Asia.

Second, it gave light. Before fire, when the sun went down, the night was simply dark, except for the moon and stars. With a fire, people had a few more hours of light in the evening. They could sit together, and work, and talk, and tell stories. Some scientists think that this gift of evening light changed human life in deep ways, giving people time together after the work of the day was done. We'll come back to that later in the night.

Third, it gave safety. Most large animals are afraid of fire. A camp with a fire in it, and people around it, was a much safer place to sleep than the open ground. Lions and hyenas still lived in Europe during much of the Ice Age, along with bears and wolves, and on a dark night, a ring of firelight was a kind of wall.

And fourth, it gave cooked food. Cooking makes food softer and easier to digest, and it releases more of its energy. Some scientists, most famously the anthropologist Richard Wrangham, have argued that cooking shaped human bodies over hundreds of thousands of years, giving us smaller jaws and teeth, smaller guts, and larger brains. That idea is still debated, especially the question of how early it began. But almost everyone agrees that cooked food mattered.

There's one more thing fire did, and it's a quiet one. It gave people something to watch. Look into the fire now. Look at the way the flames rise and curl and sink, never quite the same twice. Look at the red glow deep in the heart of the embers, pulsing slowly, brighter and dimmer, like something breathing. People have looked into fires like this for hundreds of thousands of years, at the end of every day, and their minds have grown slow and soft, and their eyes have grown heavy. Perhaps that's why so many of us still find it so restful, even now.

The young man reaches out again and turns a piece of bone with a long stick, so that a fresh side faces the heat. Sparks rise in a little cloud, bright orange, and float up toward the smoke hole, and wink out one by one. The grandmother watches them go. The baby, in her mother's arms, watches them too, her eyes wide and dark and shining.

Outside, the wind moves softly over the roof. Inside, the fire breathes.

0:27:03Supper by the Hearth · 989 words

It's time to eat.

The mother hands the baby to the grandmother for a moment, and kneels by the hearth. Near the edge of the fire, where the stones are hot but the flames don't reach, she's set several flat stones to warm, and now she lays thin strips of meat across them. The meat sizzles at once, with a soft, spitting hiss, and a smell rises up that fills the whole house. It's rich and smoky and good, and the children, who have been lying on the furs looking sleepy, sit up straight.

The meat is reindeer. Reindeer were one of the most important animals in the lives of Ice Age people across much of Europe and Asia. Their meat was food, their fat was fuel and food at once, their skins made the warmest clothing, their sinews made thread, and their antlers and bones made tools. On these plains, people also hunted horse and bison, and smaller animals like hare and arctic fox, whose fur was especially soft. And they ate mammoth, when they had it, though how often they hunted mammoths, and how often they gathered meat and bone from animals that had died in other ways, is still something archaeologists discuss.

The meat isn't the only food. In a skin bag by the wall, there's a store of dried meat, cut into thin strips and dried in the wind and smoke in the autumn, so that it keeps for months. It's hard and chewy, and very good to suck on slowly. There's fat, too, a great deal of it, rendered down from bones and stored in skin bags or in the cold earth. Fat matters more than almost anything here. In a cold climate, people need a great deal of energy just to stay warm, and lean meat on its own can't give it to them. Fat can. The talk is easy and quiet. They talk about the day. When the meal is done, nothing is wasted. The bones are gathered up and set aside. Some will be cracked for grease, boiled in a skin bag with hot stones to draw out every last bit of fat. The evening meal is over now, and the house has grown quieter. The children are full and warm, and the little girl has climbed into her mother's lap and is half asleep already, one hand curled around a fold of her mother's coat. The grandmother has taken up some work. She's sewing.

Watch her hands, because what she's doing is one of the great inventions of the human past, and without it, no one could have slept through a night like this one.

She has a piece of hide across her knees, soft and pale, scraped thin and rubbed until it's almost as supple as cloth. It's reindeer skin, with the fur still on, and she's sewing it to another piece, edge to edge. In her right hand, she holds a needle. It's small and fine, no longer than your little finger, and it's made of bone. At one end it's sharp, sharpened on a stone until the point is almost invisible. At the other end there's a tiny hole, drilled through the bone, and through that hole she's passed a thread.

The thread is made of sinew, the tough, stringy tissue that runs along an animal's spine and legs. When it's dried and pulled apart into strands, sinew makes a thread that's very strong, and it has a special quality. When it gets wet, it shrinks a little and tightens. So a seam sewn with sinew pulls itself closed, and it stays closed, even in rain and snow.

She pushes the needle through the hide, draws the thread through, and pulls it snug. Then she turns the needle and pushes it back the other way, making a tiny, even stitch. Then again. Her hands move steadily, without hurrying, and the seam grows along the edge of the hide, neat and tight. Every so often she pauses, holds the work up toward the fire, and looks along the seam to see that it's straight.

Needles with eyes in them, like this one, are a surprisingly late invention. People had been working hides for a very long time before them, using stone knives to cut and scrape, and awls, which are pointed tools, to punch holes. But a needle with an eye, that lets you draw a thread through a hole in one motion, is something else. The oldest eyed needles that have been found so far come from a place called Denisova Cave, in the mountains of southern Siberia, and the layer one of them was found in is thought to be around fifty thousand years old, though dates like these are still being refined. Needles like them turn up later at many Ice Age sites, across Europe and Asia, and some of them are so fine that the thread they carried must have been very thin indeed.

That small hole in the end of a bone needle changed what people could wear. With it, you could sew clothes that were fitted, close to the body, with seams that didn't let the wind in. You could make hoods, and mittens, and boots, and trousers. You could make clothes in layers, an inner layer of soft fur against the skin and an outer layer of tougher hide to keep off the wind and the wet. And you could repair them, over and over, so that a good coat lasted for years.

Why does this matter for sleep? Because in a climate like this one, clothing is a kind of bed that you carry with you. At night, these people didn't undress the way we do. They loosened their clothes, perhaps, and took off their boots, but they slept in their furs. The coat that kept you warm while you walked across the plain all day kept you warm while you lay down at night. We can see something of how good that skill was. In the frozen ground of Siberia, the bodies of Ice Age people have sometimes been preserved with their clothing, or with the beads that were sewn onto it. At a famous burial at a place called Sunghir, in Russia, a man and two children were buried around thirty four thousand years ago, and their clothes had been covered with thousands of tiny beads made of mammoth ivory, sewn on in patterns. Then she folds it, sets it aside, and reaches for something else. It's a small, flat lamp, carved from a piece of soft stone, and she sets it down beside her and leans toward the fire to light it. They're stuffed with dry grass, to keep the feet warm and to soak up moisture. In the morning, that grass will be taken out and dried by the fire, and fresh grass put in. It's a small thing, drying your socks by the fire, and people have been doing it, in one form or another, for tens of thousands of years.

The little girl in her mother's lap has fallen properly asleep now. Her mother shifts her gently, so that her head rests in the crook of her arm, and pulls a corner of her own fur over the child's back. The child doesn't stir. Her sleeping place is a low platform of earth and stone against the wall, covered with a thick layer of something soft. To see how long, we have to leave the Ice Age plains for a while and go back to Africa, and back in time, to a cave.

In the mountains between South Africa and the country of Eswatini, there's a cave called Border Cave, high in a cliff in the Lebombo Mountains. People lived there, on and off, for a very long time. In 2020, a team of archaeologists led by Lyn Wadley, of the University of the Witwatersrand, published a remarkable finding. Two hundred thousand years. That's more than ten times older than our house of bones tonight. The people who made those grass beds weren't quite us, or perhaps they were the very earliest of us. Our own species, Homo sapiens, seems to have appeared in Africa somewhere around three hundred thousand years ago, so these beds belong to the deep early part of our story, or to the people who came just before.

And the beds were clever. The grass was laid on top of layers of ash, the fine grey powder left by old fires. The archaeologists think this was deliberate. Ash is unpleasant for insects. It clogs their breathing, and they can't easily crawl through it, and it dries them out. So a layer of ash under your bedding was a way of keeping ticks and other biting creatures away from you while you slept. On top of the oldest grass, they also found the remains of a plant called the camphor bush, which people in parts of Africa still use today to keep insects away. Its leaves have a strong, sharp smell that many crawling things dislike.

So two hundred thousand years ago, someone was thinking about how to sleep comfortably, and how to sleep without being bitten, and was going to some trouble to arrange it. It was a kind of housekeeping, and it's one of the earliest kinds we can see.

There's more. At another cave in South Africa, called Sibudu, in a cliff above a river north of Durban, Lyn Wadley and her colleagues found bedding from about seventy seven thousand years ago. Those leaves are still used in traditional medicine. And here too, the old bedding was burned now and then, and new bedding laid down, and over thousands of years the layers built up, one on top of another, a long, quiet record of people making their beds and sleeping in them and making them again.

Think about that for a moment. The impulse to make a soft, clean, sweet-smelling place to sleep, raised up off the bare ground, sheltered from insects, isn't new at all. It's one of the oldest human habits there is. When you smooth your sheets and shake your pillow before you lie down tonight, you're doing something that people have been doing, in their own way, since before there were cities, before there was farming, before there was even, quite, us.

Back in our house, the grandmother spreads a fur over her grass mat and smooths it with her hand, the way you might smooth a blanket. She sets her lamp where she can reach it. Then she takes off her boots, pulls out the dry grass that lines them, and sets the grass near the fire to dry, but not so near that it might catch. She knows exactly how close is safe. She's been doing this all her life.

The father is doing something similar on the other side of the fire, making a place for himself and for the boy. He lays down a hide with the fur upward, so that it's soft against the skin, and he folds another one at one end, for a pillow. The boy watches him, and then lies down on it to try it, and wriggles, and declares, in whatever words they use, that it's good.

Not everyone in the deep past slept on the ground, though. In warmer times and warmer places, people slept in other ways. Some slept on raised platforms of wood or stone, to be up off the damp earth and away from snakes and insects. Some, in later ages, slept on rooftops, where the night air was cooler than the rooms below. And some peoples, right up to recent times, have slept sitting up, or leaning, or in hammocks slung above the ground. There's no single ancient way to sleep. There's only the shared habit of making, each night, the best and safest and most comfortable place you can, out of whatever the land around you offers.

The grandmother lies down. She pulls a heavy fur up over her shoulder and tucks it under her chin. For a moment she lies on her back, looking up at the bones of the roof and the haze of smoke, and at the small patch of stars she can see through the smoke hole. Then she turns onto her side, facing the fire, and closes her eyes.

But she isn't asleep yet. And neither, quite, is anyone else. Because before sleep, in this house, there's one more thing. There's a story.

0:49:00The Story by the Fire · 1,208 words

The father sits up a little, and clears his throat, and the boy, who had been nearly asleep, opens his eyes at once and turns toward him. The young man by the door sits forward too. Even the mother, with the sleeping child in her arms, shifts so that she can listen. The grandmother doesn't open her eyes, but her hand, resting on the fur, is still, and you can tell she's listening as well.

We don't know what story he tells. That's the honest truth, and it's worth pausing on. These people had language, and they had it fully. They could say anything that you or I can say. They told stories, and sang songs, and made jokes, and argued, and comforted each other, and taught their children the names of every animal and plant and star they knew. We can be sure of that, because no human group that has ever been known has done otherwise, and because the things they made, the paintings and carvings and beads, show minds as rich and as playful as ours.

But the words themselves are gone. Spoken words don't survive in the ground. They last only as long as the breath that carries them, and then they're gone, unless someone writes them down, and writing is still many thousands of years in the future. So we can never hear the stories that were told beside fires like this one, eighteen thousand years ago, or fifty thousand, or a hundred thousand. We can only know that they were told, and imagine, gently, what they might have been about.

Let's do that, softly, without pretending we know.

Perhaps he tells a story about the mammoths. Everyone who lives on this plain lives alongside them, and thinks about them, and depends on them, for meat and fat and bone and hide and ivory. Perhaps the story is about where the mammoths go in the winter, and why they return in the spring, and about a person, long ago, who followed them farther than anyone had followed them before, and came back with news of a warm valley beyond the ice. Stories like that are useful. They carry knowledge, about the land and the animals and the seasons, wrapped in a shape that's easy to remember and pleasant to hear.

Or perhaps he tells a story about the stars. Look up through the smoke hole. The sky tonight is extraordinarily clear, and the stars are bright and sharp, far brighter than they look above any town or city today, because there's no other light in the whole world to compete with them. The band of the Milky Way runs across the sky like a river of pale light. These people see this sky every clear night of their lives, and they know it the way you know the streets of your own town. They know which stars rise first in the evening at this time of year, and which are still there at dawn, and how the whole pattern turns, slowly, through the night and through the seasons. They've given names to the bright ones, and made shapes out of them, and told stories about those shapes. We don't know their names or their shapes. But the sky they looked at is the same sky, and the turning of it is the same turning.

Or perhaps, and this is the kind of story told most often beside fires, in every part of the world, he tells a story about people. About a grandmother who was cleverer than a wolf. About two brothers who argued over a reindeer and what became of them. About a child who wandered away from the camp and how she found her way home by the sound of the river. Stories about people are how a group remembers who it is, and how it teaches the young what's brave and what's foolish and what's kind.

The father's voice is low and steady, pitched just above the crackle of the fire. He uses his hands a little as he speaks. The boy's eyes are wide and shining in the firelight, and his lips move sometimes, shaping a word he knows is coming. He's heard this story before. He wants to hear it again. That's how stories work, and how they've always worked. The ones you love, you want told exactly the same way, every time.

Now, here's something that scientists have thought carefully about. The anthropologist Polly Wiessner spent many years with the Ju/'hoansi people of the Kalahari, in southern Africa, who until recent times lived by hunting and gathering, and she listened closely to their talk. She found something striking. By day, their conversation was mostly practical. It was about work, and food, and where to go, and who had said what. But at night, in the firelight, the talk changed. At night, more than four fifths of their conversation was stories. Stories about people they knew, and about people long gone, and about spirits, and about the doings of the wider world. The night talk was where news travelled, where conflicts were aired and settled, where the imagination wandered, and where the group, gathered close around the fire, felt itself to be one thing.

Wiessner suggested that the control of fire, and the gift of firelight in the evening, may have been what made this possible, far back in the human past. The day is for work. The night, once you have a fire to see by and to gather around, is for everything else. For stories, and music, and laughter, and the slow, wandering talk that binds people together. It's a powerful idea, and it fits with what we see in so many places. But it's an idea about the past built from watching the present, and we should hold it gently. We can't go back and listen at a fire a hundred thousand years ago. We can only notice that wherever people have firelight and time, this is what they seem to do with it.

The father's story is coming to its end. His voice drops a little, and slows, and the boy, whose eyes have been growing heavier and heavier, lets them close. He doesn't want to. He wants to hear the ending. But the warmth, and the full stomach, and the low voice, and the long day, are stronger than he is, and between one sentence and the next, he's asleep.

The father finishes the story anyway, quietly, for the others, and for himself. Then he sits for a moment, looking into the fire, and then he lies down beside his son and pulls the fur up over them both.

0:57:19Nests in the Trees · 1,017 words

While the house settles into sleep, let's drift a long way back again, further than the grass beds of Border Cave, further than the first fires. Let's ask where human sleep began.

To do that, we have to go to the forests of Africa, and look up into the trees.

It's evening in a forest, somewhere in the centre of the continent, and the light is green and gold, filtering down through layer after layer of leaves. High in the branches of a tall tree, perhaps fifty or sixty feet above the ground, a chimpanzee is making her bed.

She does it quickly and with great skill. She finds a fork where several strong branches meet. She reaches out and bends the nearest branches inward, one after another, folding them across each other and pressing them down with her feet, so that they make a firm platform, like the frame of a basket. Then she pulls in smaller branches and leafy twigs and tucks them around the edges, and breaks off a few soft, leafy sprays and lays them in the middle, for a pillow or a mattress. The whole thing takes her only a few minutes. Then she lies down in it, on her side or her back, and pulls a last leafy branch over herself, and settles in for the night.

Chimpanzees do this every single evening. So do bonobos, and gorillas, and orangutans, our closest living relatives among the great apes. Each of them builds a fresh bed for every night, and they almost never use the same one twice. Young apes learn how to do it by watching their mothers, and it takes them years to get it right. Their first nests are clumsy and lopsided, and they often end up sleeping in their mother's nest instead, curled against her, until they're four or five years old.

Scientists who've studied these nests have found that they're surprisingly well made. Chimpanzees seem to choose particular kinds of trees, with strong, springy branches. Orangutans sometimes build roofs over their nests to keep off the rain. And there's some evidence that sleeping in a well-built nest, high above the ground, away from insects and predators, lets an ape sleep more deeply and more soundly than it could on a bare branch. Studies of orangutans sleeping in their nests found just that.

Because humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor, who lived in Africa something like six to seven million years ago, many scientists think that the habit of making a bed each night is very old indeed. The ancestor we share with the apes probably built nests too. So when you make your bed tonight, you're doing something that may be not tens of thousands, but millions of years old. It may be one of the oldest things you ever do.

Then something changed. Over millions of years, the human line came down from the trees. Our ancestors began to walk upright on two legs, and to spend more and more of their time on the ground, out in the open woodlands and grasslands. Their feet changed, losing the grasping big toe that's so useful for climbing. Their bodies grew taller and longer legged, made for walking and running over long distances. And at some point, they stopped sleeping in the trees.

When exactly did that happen? No one can say for sure. Beds of leaves don't leave fossils. But some of the earliest members of the human family, the ones called australopithecines, such as the famous skeleton known as Lucy, who lived more than three million years ago, still had long arms and curved fingers, good for climbing. Many scientists think they still climbed into trees to sleep at night, for safety, even if they walked on the ground by day. Later species, especially the one called Homo erectus, which appeared nearly two million years ago, had bodies much more like ours, built for life on the ground, and they were probably sleeping on the ground, at least some of the time.

Sleeping on the ground is dangerous, of course, if you're out in the open, among lions and leopards and hyenas. So what made it possible? Most likely, a combination of things. Sleeping together, in groups. Choosing safe places, such as rock shelters and caves, or thick bushes. And eventually, fire.

The anthropologist David Samson and his colleagues have put forward an interesting idea about this. They've compared human sleep with the sleep of other primates, and found that humans are unusual. We sleep less than almost any other primate. Many monkeys and apes sleep for ten, twelve, or even more hours in a day. Humans, on average, sleep about seven. But our sleep is unusually deep, and an unusually large part of it is the kind of sleep called REM sleep, the stage of sleep in which most vivid dreaming happens.

Samson has suggested that this might be connected to the move from trees to ground. Once our ancestors were sleeping on the ground, close together, perhaps beside a fire, with someone awake to keep watch, they could afford to sleep more deeply, and they didn't need to sleep for so long. A shorter, deeper, more dream-filled sleep would have left more hours of the day, and the evening, for other things, for learning and making and talking. It's an idea, not a certainty, and other scientists have questioned parts of it. But it's a lovely one to think about, here, beside the fire. That the shape of our own sleep, short and deep and full of dreams, may have been shaped by the very things around us in this house. By the fire, and the shelter, and the closeness of other people.

Back in the house of bones, nobody is thinking about any of this. The fire is low. The sleepers are still. The little girl turns over in her sleep, makes a small sound, and pushes one arm out from under the fur. Her mother, without fully waking, reaches over and tucks it back in.

Some things haven't changed at all.

Let's look around the house now, in the low red light, and see how everyone is sleeping.

They're sleeping close. The house is small, and there are eight people in it, and they lie near enough to each other that, if any one of them stretched out an arm, they'd touch someone else. The mother lies with the baby tucked against her chest, and the little girl curled at her back. The father lies with the boy beside him. The young man lies near the door, between the sleepers and the cold. The grandmother lies closest to the fire. Everyone's feet point, roughly, toward the hearth, where the warmth is.

This closeness is ordinary for almost every human who has ever lived. The idea of a person sleeping alone, in a room of their own, in a bed of their own, is quite a new one, and even today it isn't how most of the world sleeps. Through most of the human past, people slept in families, in groups, in shared spaces, often in a shared bed, or on a shared floor. It was warmer that way. It was safer that way. And for most people, it was simply the natural way to be.

Babies, especially, slept with their mothers. A mother on the mammoth steppe, eighteen thousand years ago, wouldn't have dreamed of putting her baby to sleep anywhere but beside her, against her body, in the warmth of her furs. And all through the night, without really waking, she'd feed the baby when it stirred, and settle it, and sleep again. Anthropologists who've studied mothers and babies in many traditional societies have found that this is how it's done in most of them, and it's very likely that it has been this way for a very long time.

Closeness is warmth, too, and on a night like this one, warmth matters very much. Outside, the temperature is falling steadily. On a clear, still night in the Ice Age, on these plains, it may well have dropped to twenty degrees below freezing, perhaps much colder. No one can measure that night exactly, so think of this as a fair guess. Inside, it's much warmer. The walls of hide and earth hold the heat in. The floor, dug into the ground, is sheltered from the wind. The fire gives off its steady glow. And the bodies of eight people, each one giving off about as much heat as a small lamp, add up to a great deal of warmth in a small space.

So each sleeper is wrapped in layers. Closest to the skin, their own soft inner clothing of fur, worn with the hair turned inward. Over that, perhaps, a sleeping robe or a heavy fur thrown across them. Under them, the grass mat and the hides. Around them, the warm air of the house. And beside them, the warmth of another body. Each layer traps a little more warm air, and the sleeper inside all those layers, breathing slowly, is as warm as you are in your own bed tonight.

Listen to the house now. Listen carefully, because it's full of small sounds.

There's the fire, of course. It's quieter than it was earlier in the evening. The flames have sunk down, and now it's mostly embers, glowing red and orange, with a few small blue flames running over them and vanishing. Now and then a piece of bone shifts, or a stick breaks in two, with a soft crunch, and sends up a few sparks.

There's the breathing of the sleepers. Eight people, all breathing at slightly different speeds. The quick, light breath of the baby. The slow, deep breath of the father. The grandmother, who breathes very quietly, so that you have to listen hard to hear her at all. And the young man by the door, who snores, very softly, a low, rumbling sound, like a cat purring a long way off.

There's the wind over the roof. It's a gentle wind tonight, and it makes only a small, whispering sound as it passes over the smoke hole, and a faint creak, now and then, from the hides that cover the walls, as they shift against the bones.

And there are the small, private sounds of sleep. Someone turns over and sighs. Someone murmurs a word in their sleep and is quiet again. Someone's foot moves under a fur, with a soft rustle of hide against hide. These are the sounds that every human night has been full of, in every house and every shelter and every camp, for as long as there have been people to make them.

The dog has come in, too. It came in quietly a little while ago, pushing through the hides at the door, and now it's curled up in a tight ball beside the young man, its nose tucked under its tail, its thick coat rising and falling. Its ears twitch now and then at a sound from outside. Then it settles again.

Not everyone in the camp is asleep.

In the house next to ours, an older man is sitting up by his fire. He's wrapped in a heavy robe, with his knees drawn up and his arms around them, and he's looking into the embers, wide awake. He isn't anxious, and he isn't on guard, exactly. He just isn't sleepy. He went to sleep early in the evening, before the stories were finished, and now, in the middle of the night, he's woken, as he often does, and he's sitting by the fire for a while, keeping it alive, listening to the night.

Every so often he reaches for a stick and lays it on the embers, and watches the flame catch. Every so often he lifts his head, and listens, when a sound comes from outside. Then he settles again. In a while, he'll lie down and sleep some more. And then, in the small hours, someone else will be awake. A young mother, perhaps, feeding her baby. Or a teenager, who went to bed late and is still restless. And so, all through the night, without anyone planning it, there will almost always be someone awake somewhere in the camp.

That might sound like a picture we've invented. In a sense it is. But it's based on something scientists have actually measured.

In 2017, David Samson and a team of researchers published a study of sleep among the Hadza. The Hadza are a people of northern Tanzania, in East Africa, who live in the dry country around a lake called Lake Eyasi. They're modern people, living in the modern world, with their own history, and their way of life has changed and is still changing. The researchers asked thirty three Hadza adults in one camp to wear small devices on their wrists, a little like a watch, that recorded every movement they made, through the night, for about three weeks. From those movements, it's possible to tell, roughly, whether someone is awake or asleep. Then the researchers lined up all the records, night by night, minute by minute.

What they found was remarkable. Over twenty nights, there were only eighteen minutes, in total, when everyone wearing a device was asleep at the same time. Eighteen minutes, in twenty nights. For all the rest of the night, someone, somewhere in the camp, was awake, or at least sleeping only very lightly. Usually, it was quite a few people. On a typical night, at any given moment, about eight of them were awake or lightly asleep.

The reason, the researchers found, wasn't that people were taking turns on purpose. Nobody set a watch. It was simply that different people kept different hours. Older people tended to go to sleep early and wake early. Younger adults tended to go to sleep late and wake late. Some people woke briefly several times in the night. And because the camp was a mix of ages, young and old and in between, their different rhythms overlapped, and between them they covered almost the whole night.

The researchers called this sentinel-like behaviour. A sentinel is a guard, someone who keeps watch. And their idea was that this mixing of different sleep patterns in a group might have been useful, over the long human past. When people slept together in small groups, with grandparents and parents and teenagers and children all together, there would almost always be someone awake, or nearly awake, who could notice if the fire was dying, or a storm was coming, or an animal was prowling near. No one had to lose sleep. No one had to stand guard. The watch just happened, naturally, because people are different.

It's an idea that might change how you think about your own nights. If you're someone who goes to bed early and wakes before dawn, or someone who can't sleep until long after midnight, or someone who wakes for a while in the middle of the night, you might have been, in a camp like this one, exactly the person the group needed. Your restlessness might have been a gift.

We should be careful, of course. This is one study, of one group of people, in one place, over a few weeks. It tells us something real about how the Hadza in that camp slept. Whether it tells us how people slept eighteen thousand years ago, on the cold plains of Europe, is something we can only suppose. But it's a reasonable and a gentle supposition, and it fits the picture we have. A small camp, a ring of houses, fires that need tending, and people of all ages, sleeping and waking, each in their own rhythm, through the night.

The older man stands in the doorway, and the cold air flows in past him, and he looks out at the night. Let's leave him there for a little while, looking at the stars, and think about another study of sleep, a larger one, because it tells us something lovely about the shape of a human night.

In 2015, a team of researchers led by Gandhi Yetish and Jerome Siegel, at the University of California, Los Angeles, published the results of a careful study. They wanted to answer a question that many people had wondered about. How did humans sleep before electric light, before clocks and alarms and screens? Did we sleep longer? Did we sleep differently?

Of course, they couldn't go back in time. So instead, they went to three groups of people who still live without electricity and in ways that are closer to the old ways than most of us. One group was the Hadza, in Tanzania, whom we've already met. The second was a group of San people in Namibia, in southern Africa. And the third was the Tsimane, a people who live by farming, fishing and hunting in the forests of Bolivia, in South America.

These are three very different peoples, living on two different continents, with different languages, histories and ways of life. The researchers asked volunteers in each group to wear small devices on their wrists that recorded their movement, and the light around them, and in some cases the temperature of their skin and the air nearby. Then they gathered many nights of records, in summer and in winter.

What they found surprised a lot of people.

First, these people didn't sleep more than people in industrial countries. Many had expected that, freed from electric light and busy schedules, people would sleep for nine or ten hours. But they didn't. On average, they slept between about five and three quarters and seven hours a night. That's at the lower end of what people sleep in cities today. They did spend longer in bed, or on their sleeping mats, than they slept, perhaps seven to eight and a half hours from when they settled down to when they got up. But the actual sleep was about the same as ours, or a little less.

Second, they didn't go to sleep when the sun went down. On average, they went to sleep about three and a quarter hours after sunset. The hours of early darkness were spent awake, by the fire, talking, working, telling stories, just as in our house of bones. And they usually woke before the sun came up.

Third, and this is the part that's most beautiful, their sleep seemed to follow the temperature. All three groups tended to fall asleep as the night air was growing cooler, and to wake up close to the coldest point of the night, which comes just before dawn. As the air cooled through the night, their bodies cooled with it. Then, near the coldest point, the small blood vessels in their hands and feet tightened, drawing warmth back into the body, and they woke. The researchers suggested that this daily rise and fall of the air's temperature, which most of us have shut out with our heated and cooled houses, might be one of nature's own signals for sleep.

There were a few other small things. Very few people in these groups had trouble sleeping, and most didn't even have a word for that kind of trouble. People slept about an hour longer in winter than in summer. And they napped less than you might think, on fewer than a quarter of days even in summer.

But there was one more finding, and it bears directly on a question we'll come to in a moment. In all three groups, the researchers found that sleep, once it began, mostly continued through the night. People woke briefly, now and then, as everyone does, but they didn't usually wake for a long stretch of an hour or more in the middle of the night and then go back to sleep.

Here, though, we must be careful, as the researchers themselves were careful. It would be easy to say that these peoples are a window onto the deep past, and that their sleep is how all humans slept before modern life. That would be too much. The Hadza, the San and the Tsimane are modern people. They have their own histories, and many of them have contact with towns and markets and modern goods. They live in warm places, near the equator or in the tropics, where the nights are about the same length all year round. The people in our house of bones live in a very cold place, far to the north, where winter nights are long, perhaps fifteen or sixteen hours of darkness. Their nights might have been different in all sorts of ways.

So what these studies give us isn't a photograph of the past. It's something more modest and, in a way, more comforting. They show us that a human night, without electric light, in a small group, near a fire, tends to have a certain gentle shape. A long, wakeful evening by the fire. Sleep that comes as the air cools. A few brief wakings, and someone almost always stirring. And a waking in the cold, still hour before dawn. That shape seems to be shared by people who live very far apart, and it may be very old indeed.

There's a question that many people ask when they wonder how our ancestors slept, and it's worth taking slowly. Did people once sleep in two parts?

The idea comes from the work of a historian named Roger Ekirch. In the 1990s and early two thousands, Ekirch was studying how people in Europe lived at night, in the centuries before electric light. He read hundreds and hundreds of old documents, diaries, letters, court records, medical books, prayer books and poems, many of them from the 1500s to the 1800s. And again and again, he kept coming across a curious phrase. People wrote about their first sleep. And they wrote about their second sleep.

As Ekirch pieced it together, it seemed that in many parts of Europe, people commonly went to bed a few hours after dark, slept for a few hours, and then woke, around the middle of the night. They were awake for an hour or so, sometimes more. And then they went back to sleep until morning. That middle time of waking was so ordinary that it didn't need explaining. People used it to pray, or to think, or to tend the fire, or to talk quietly with whoever was beside them, or to make love, or to visit a neighbour, or simply to lie in the dark and rest. Some people called it the watch. In his book, published in 2005, Ekirch called this pattern segmented sleep.

There's some support for the idea from a very different direction, too. In the early 1990s, a psychiatrist named Thomas Wehr, at the National Institutes of Health in the United States, ran an experiment. He asked a small group of volunteers to spend fourteen hours each night in darkness, for several weeks, as if they were living through the long nights of winter without any artificial light. After a while, many of the volunteers' sleep changed shape. They began to sleep in two parts, with a quiet time of waking in between, lasting an hour or more, during which they felt calm and peaceful. It was a small study, and how much it tells us about everyday life in the past is still debated.

So some people have suggested that two sleeps might be the natural way for humans to sleep, and that the single long block of sleep that many of us aim for today is a modern invention, brought about by electric light and the pressures of industrial work. That's a comforting idea for those of us who wake in the middle of the night. It suggests that there's nothing wrong with us, that we're simply doing what our ancestors did.

But, as so often, the full picture is less tidy.

Remember the study of the Hadza, the San and the Tsimane. In all three groups, the researchers found no clear sign of two separate sleeps. People slept, for the most part, in a single stretch, with only brief wakings. That surprised many people, and it led to a lively debate. Did it mean that segmented sleep wasn't natural after all? Or did it mean something else?

One suggestion was that it might depend on circumstances. In the tropics, where those three groups live, nights are about twelve hours long all year round. In northern Europe, in winter, nights can last sixteen hours or more. With so many hours of darkness, people may have slept in two parts simply because there was so much night to fill. Ekirch himself didn't accept that. He pointed out that people in early modern Europe described a first and second sleep in every season, not just in winter, and he gathered accounts of a similar pattern from many other parts of the world. Others have suggested that cold, or the shape of the working day, or other features of life in early modern Europe, might have played a part. The debate isn't settled.

So where does that leave us, on this long winter night on the mammoth steppe, eighteen thousand years ago?

The honest answer is that we don't know. Nobody wrote anything down. There are no diaries from the Ice Age. We can't measure the sleep of people who lived so long ago. All we can do is put together what we know, gently, and see what seems likely.

Here's what seems likely. These people lived far to the north, and in winter their nights were very long. They had fire, and lamps, but only a little light, and fuel was precious. They slept in small groups, with people of all ages, in warm, close shelters. And they had no clocks, no alarms, nowhere to be at any particular hour. In a world like that, it seems likely that sleep was flexible. On some nights, perhaps, they slept in one long stretch. On others, especially in the depths of winter, perhaps they woke in the middle of the night, for a while, and tended the fire, and talked softly, and then slept again. And on any night, someone would be awake, and someone asleep, and the fire would be fed.

What all of this suggests, more than anything, is that there's no single right way to sleep. Humans have slept in one stretch and in two, early and late, alone and together, in many different ways, depending on where and how they lived. If you sometimes wake in the night, and lie for a while in the dark before sleep comes back, you're in very good company. People have been doing exactly that for a very, very long time.

But that's for another day. Tonight, they're still here, in their round house of bones, under the stars, beside the fire.

And they've left us something. Every time you make your bed at the end of the day, smoothing the covers, plumping the pillow, making a soft, clean place to rest, you're doing what people did two hundred thousand years ago in a cave in Africa, and what our ancestors may have done in the trees, long before that. Every time you sit by a fire, or a candle, or even a softly glowing lamp, and feel your mind grow slow and quiet, you're doing what people have done since fire first came into human hands. And every time you wake for a while in the middle of the night, and lie listening in the dark, and drift back to sleep, you're keeping the oldest watch there is.

Let the fire burn low now, softly, far away. Let the crackle of the sticks slow and fade. Let the warmth settle over you like a heavy, soft fur. Let the breathing of the sleepers around you become your own breathing, slow and deep and even, rising and settling, rising and settling, the way it did for every sleeper in that small round house, all through the night.

The fire is still alight. All is well.

Next time, we go in search of lost cities.

Sleep well. Safe travels through the night.
